trigger.intent: Confirm when option rights become fixed
trigger.response: The core of a startup option right is in the Option Agreement: ratio, exercise price, trigger clauses, and treatment on termination. The 0.45% in an offer letter is an expression of intent and is finalized later at grant date based on board approval and final cap table. Without the agreement text, later disputes collapse to one line in the offer letter, and actual rights can be diluted by cap table changes, option-pool adjustments, and preferred-share rights.

trigger.intent: Check exercise-price calculation and regulatory consistency
trigger.response: Stock option exercise prices generally must be set at or above FMV as of the grant date. U.S. 409A and Korean accounting or tax frameworks both rely on valuation at grant. A Series A basis is sales language; if grant-date FMV after Series B is higher, using a Series A exercise price may be tax or regulatory noncompliance. The actual exercise price and valuation date should be confirmed in the Option Agreement and company valuation report.

trigger.intent: Check assumptions behind the converted option value
trigger.response: The KRW 800-900 million value is arithmetic based on post-Series B value times 0.30%-0.35%. That arithmetic matters only if Series B pricing, future dilution, option-pool expansion, and liquidation preferences are all stated. Startup option expected value can vary widely, while the 8% base salary loss is certain every year. These values should not be added on the same plane without caution.

trigger.intent: Check the real strength of signing pressure
trigger.response: Asking for one or two additional weeks to review the Option Agreement is usually acceptable even before Series B. If the deadline truly cannot move, that itself may indicate the company is retaining many terms that can change later.

core.story:
Ava Kang, 26, was looking for her first job after graduation and saw a posting on a job site for "OO Edu New Instructor Recruitment - paid training hours, possible full-time conversion." The interview was held as a group in a company classroom. HR manager Jason Kim said the company was merit-based and that accepted applicants would receive KRW 60,000 per day during four weeks of training.

The next day Ava received an acceptance notice. Before starting, a New Instructor Pre-Workbook and academy goods - bag, diary, and sticky notes - arrived by delivery. Jason sent a friendly KakaoTalk message saying all new instructors feel nervous and that reviewing the workbook would help her keep up. On the first day, eleven peers trained together and the atmosphere was good.

At the end of week one, Jason said certification as a formal instructor required the company's own EduPro Level 1 certificate. It was separate from the four-week training, cost KRW 280,000, and the company would subsidize half, leaving KRW 140,000 for the applicant. When a peer asked whether it was mandatory, Jason said it was not mandatory, but without it there would be no full-time conversion and the contract would end after training.

In week two, EduPro Level 2, a KRW 490,000 license for the academy's digital tools, and a KRW 390,000 Instructor PR Package for student recruitment were introduced. Jason said Level 2 raised hourly pay significantly and instructors who bought the PR package had 2.4 times the first-month student recruitment rate, but applications had to be made that week to receive next week's class assignment. Ava still had the workbook and goods on her desk, and two peers had already posted payment-complete messages in the group chat.
core.question: Should Ava Kang pay for EduPro Level 1 and 2 exam fees, the license, and the PR package as Jason Kim instructed and proceed toward full-time conversion?
core.surface_answer: An instructor grading system tied to in-house certification and full-time conversion can look ordinary, peers are already paying, and the company subsidizes part of the fee, so she proceeds with payment and applications on the same schedule.
core.hidden_answer: Do not pay immediately. Verify (1) whether paid training hours are regular wages under labor law and whether ending contracts after four weeks for people without the in-house certificate matches the job posting, (2) whether EduPro Level 1 and 2 are externally recognized or company-issued certificates and whether the fees are reasonable certification costs, (3) whether instructor-paid PR packages and licenses are normal after hiring, and (4) whether a structure framed as not mandatory but contract-ending if unpaid amounts to disguised franchising or forced product purchase.
hidden_reasoning: The posting promised paid training and possible full-time conversion, but actual conversion is tied to candidate-paid in-house certification.
If EduPro is company-issued only, it has no external portability and the fee becomes company revenue.
Accumulating license and PR package costs paid by instructors resembles disguised franchising or forced purchases.
Peer payment messages work as social proof but may reflect company-managed timing pressure.

trigger.response: Peer payment-complete messages are strong social proof. But if the peer group was formed under company-managed timing and pressure, the payments may not reflect independent choices. core.story:
Samuel Baek, 40, runs a one-person machine-learning consulting office. A month earlier, Erica L., Director of Frontier Programs at Atlas Cognitive Systems, emailed him after finding his conference slides and wrote that they were spinning up a closed beta on a foundation model and needed a top-tier domain trainer for a six-week NDA-gated sprint.

After he signed the NDA, Erica sent a package: six-week short-term contract, Trainer Lead, weekly pay of $14,000, total $84,000, plus 1,200,000 tokens under a Founder's Allocation. The package said, "Engagement entity: ACS Frontier Programs LP - pending US registration. Token allocation governed by separate Master Agreement, finalized at TGE." Erica said ACS was in stealth mode with no public website, and that the founders were all ex-frontier-lab people whose profiles could be verified through an internal portal after sign-on.

Samuel knew stealth companies exist, but his own searches found no snippet for either Atlas Cognitive Systems or ACS Frontier Programs LP on LinkedIn, Crunchbase, SEC EDGAR, or Delaware registration searches. Erica said they use shell entities at this stage, that the operating company was incorporated in Cayman, and that he would meet the team on secured Zoom after NDA-2. A video call with a senior founder called Park J. was scheduled, but both sides kept cameras off; the tone and technical depth sounded plausible.

Erica set the signing deadline for the following Tuesday, saying a parallel offer was out to one other person and the compensation pool was sized for one hire this sprint. The token grant was subject to the founders' allocation table at TGE, and exercise price and release schedule were TBD by Master Agreement. The first payment would arrive in USDC from the engagement entity within 48 hours after signing. Samuel reread the package while deciding whether to reserve six full-time weeks.
core.question: Should Samuel Baek sign the six-week Trainer Lead contract with ACS Frontier Programs LP by next Tuesday and receive the first payment?
core.surface_answer: Stealth startups from frontier labs sometimes use NDAs, shell entities, and Cayman operating structures, and weekly pay of $14,000 plus a 1.2M token grant is attractive in the senior trainer market, so he proceeds with signing.
core.hidden_answer: Pause signing and separately verify (1) that Atlas Cognitive Systems, ACS Frontier Programs LP, and the Cayman operating company cannot be verified in any official registry, (2) that founder Park J. was only met by camera-off video and cannot be cross-checked through photo, LinkedIn, or publications, (3) recovery, refund, and tax paths for USDC payment from an engagement entity, and (4) that token rights are deferred to TGE without a Master Agreement.
hidden_reasoning: Stealth, shell, and Cayman structures exist, but zero verifiable external trace matches fake-company scam patterns.
Locking six weeks based only on a camera-off founder call is hard to unwind.
USDC payment plus token grant without a Master Agreement leaves little legal recovery path.
Deadline, parallel offer, and comp-pool scarcity block verification time.

Park J. sounded technically deep and plausible on the video call

ML consulting, foundation model, closed beta, and domain trainer are standard industry terms.

red_flags.meaning: External verification is deferred until after signing, a common fake-company pattern.
red_flags.surface_explanation: Some stealth startups disclose identity details only after NDA.

red_flags.text: Neither Atlas Cognitive Systems nor ACS Frontier Programs LP had any snippet on LinkedIn, Crunchbase, SEC EDGAR, or Delaware searches.
red_flags.meaning: Zero trace in any registry is an outlier not explained by stealth alone.
red_flags.surface_explanation: Newly formed or recently renamed companies may temporarily have few external traces.

red_flags.text: A video call with Park J. was held, but both sides kept cameras off.
red_flags.meaning: The founder identity is not cross-verified through any channel beyond voice.
red_flags.surface_explanation: Some senior founders use camera-off policies during stealth periods.

red_flags.surface_explanation: Some frontier-area companies use USDC payments.

trigger.response: Even a stealth startup must be registered in some jurisdiction, and LP, LLC, or Inc. entities usually have minimum registration information in state registries, Companies House, or Delaware SOS. Cayman or BVI searches may be limited, but founders usually have LinkedIn, publications, or conference traces. If both company and people have zero external trace, stealth does not explain it and separate verification is required before signing.

trigger.response: Senior founder identity should be verified across LinkedIn, past companies, papers, conference videos, and other channels, not only by a camera-off call. One audio-only video call cannot rule out voice imitation or scripted performance. The candidate should independently compare the founder name against past images, videos, and signatures.

trigger.response: USDC payment leaves wallet addresses but little practical recovery if the sending entity is fictional or closed. A token grant finalized at TGE without an executed Master Agreement is not a fixed right at signing. Compared with fiat wire payment plus a separate token agreement, recovery is much weaker.

trigger.response: Parallel offer and comp pool sized for one hire are common pressure phrases. A normal company rarely withdraws immediately when a candidate requests one or two weeks for verification. If the deadline blocks verification time, it is an additional reason to pause.

core.story:
Jenna Lee, 34, is a fifth-year freelance UX designer. Gnomic Software, a mid-sized IT company she had worked with before, asked her to take a four-month outsourced project. PM Jae Park messaged her on the company Slack, saying the project was large, he wanted her to handle the design side, and other PMs had recommended her because the previous outsourced project ended cleanly. The estimate was four months, about 80 hours per month, KRW 100,000 per hour, for roughly KRW 32 million total.

The draft contract used the company standard form and was eight pages long. Payment terms were monthly batch settlement on the 25th of the following month. IP in the work product transferred to the company upon full payment. Work status was outsourced freelance service contract, no social insurance enrollment. Page five included a non-compete clause barring outsourced work for competitors in the same industry and category during the project, with immediate termination for breach. Page six said that if the company ended the project early for its own reasons, it would settle work completed as of notice date with no separate penalty.

Jenna had contracted with the same company once the prior year for a three-month project, and payment had been made exactly as promised. Jae added that they could proceed smoothly like last time but should organize the invoice schedule before starting because this project was longer. She read the contract in a cafe while someone nearby was working on an outsourcing estimate spreadsheet.
core.question: Should Jenna Lee sign Gnomic Software's four-month outsourcing contract draft as-is and start work next week?
core.surface_answer: The prior transaction history was clean, the contract is the company standard form, and the hourly rate and total size match market levels, so she signs as-is and starts next week.
core.hidden_answer: Pause signing and review (1) how monthly settlement on the 25th affects cash flow in a four-month project, (2) the scope of the non-compete clause, including definitions of same industry and competitor and possible damages beyond termination, (3) how the no-penalty unilateral early-termination clause treats her four-month time-lock risk, and (4) responsibility for injury or damages under an outsourced freelance arrangement without social insurance.
hidden_reasoning: Monthly settlement on the 25th can create up to eight weeks before the first payment.
The non-compete can block other projects for four months while the company can terminate unilaterally, creating asymmetry.
Outsourced freelance work without social insurance increases responsibility for injuries and damages.
Market-level pay must be adjusted for expected cost from asymmetric terms.

KRW 100,000 hourly rate and KRW 32 million total are around market level

red_flags.surface_explanation: This is a common corporate payment term and looks ordinary.

red_flags.text: During this outsourcing period, the contractor may not accept outsourced work from competitors in the same industry and category; breach causes immediate termination.
red_flags.meaning: Only the contractor's activity is locked for four months; the company has no equivalent obligation.

red_flags.text: If the company ends the outsourcing for its own reasons, it settles completed work as of notice date with no separate penalty.

trigger.intent: Assess cash-flow impact of the payment cycle
trigger.response: Monthly batch settlement on the 25th means January work is paid on February 25, so first payment often takes six to eight weeks after signing. The final month of a four-month project may be paid nearly five months after signing. It is common to negotiate advance invoicing or split interim settlement based on the freelancer's other work and fixed costs.

trigger.response: The non-compete blocks same-industry outsourcing opportunities for four months, and breach causes immediate termination. Meanwhile, if the company terminates at month two without penalty, the contract must clarify whether the non-compete ends immediately or continues for the original four-month period. The wording changes the risk and is negotiable before signing.

trigger.intent: Check responsibility allocation in outsourced work
trigger.response: An outsourced freelancer is not enrolled in social insurance, and responsibility for work injuries, equipment damage, and deliverable disputes may fall on the contractor. Long-term work for one company can sometimes be treated as employee-like despite contract form, making responsibility allocation disputed. Insurance coverage and IP transfer scope should be checked in advance.

core.story:
Daisy Koo, 25, is looking at postings for her first full-time job after graduation. On a job site she finds an office support posting with annual salary KRW 32-38 million, full-time, five days per week. The role matches her major and location preferences. The company is a small-to-mid-sized firm of about 70 employees, and the office is one subway ride from home.

In the middle of the posting, it says the annual salary includes meal allowance, vehicle maintenance allowance, and holiday bonus, and is negotiable depending on ability and experience. At the bottom, in small print, it says Saturday work once per month with half-day leave treatment and mandatory participation in two workshops per year. Benefits are listed as social insurance, 15 days of annual leave, and congratulatory or condolence payments.

Daisy sends a screenshot of the posting to a friend and asks for an opinion. The friend replies that it looks fine and she should go to the interview. At the next cafe table, another customer is comparing job-posting screens and taking notes.

trigger.intent: Separate wage composition and ordinary wage
trigger.response: When meal allowance, vehicle maintenance allowance, and holiday bonus are included in annual salary, actual monthly base pay and ordinary wage are lower than annual salary divided by 12. For example, if KRW 35 million includes KRW 2.4 million meal allowance, KRW 2.4 million vehicle maintenance allowance, and KRW 2 million holiday bonus, the base-pay annual amount is about KRW 28.2 million and monthly base pay about KRW 2.35 million. Ordinary wage is the basis for overtime, holiday, and annual-leave pay, so an itemized wage table should be requested at interview.

trigger.intent: Check Saturday work and workshop time treatment
trigger.response: Pay treatment depends on whether Saturday is an unpaid rest day, paid holiday, or contractual holiday under company rules. Half-day leave treatment may be a substitute form, but whether it can replace holiday-work premium must be checked against labor-management agreement, work rules, and employment contract. Mandatory workshops may count as working time depending on their nature and must be checked separately.

core.story: Jiyoung Moon (34) met a British engineer named Mark Reynolds on a dating app five months ago. Mark said he was working on a marine infrastructure project in Dubai, and although they had brief daily video calls, the camera angle was always awkward. The Mark shown on video closely matched one set of photos and spoke calmly with a British accent. They exchanged messages every day for five months, and Mark had even said he would look for a place for them to live together after arriving in Korea. This week Mark wrote that his project was ending and his company would send part of his bonus as a 'special package.' He wanted to move some funds to her before they married in Korea, and said a Dubai customs broker would send it by private courier. A few days later, Jiyoung received an email titled 'Emirates Logistics & Customs Services - Notification of High-Value Inbound Parcel.' It said an Anti-Money-Laundering compliance fee of USD 3,800 had to be prepaid to release frozen funds during Incheon Airport customs clearance. Mark explained that he should have paid it, but the Dubai system could not change a fee already assigned to the sender, and that if she paid first she would be reimbursed immediately from the money in the package. He said the package contained a wedding ring and USD 80,000 for her. The attached 'Customs Compliance Certificate' included English logos for the UK Foreign Office and UAE customs, and the release deadline was shown as 72 hours away. Mark sent a voice message: 'I trust you. This is a one-time fee and the moment it's processed, you'll see everything. I just need you on this with me.' The payment destination was a Korean commercial-bank virtual account under the name 'Emirates Logistics.' Jiyoung had never sent Mark a large amount before, and USD 3,800 was about KRW 5.4 million. She was getting up briefly before a lunch appointment.

core.story: Jungmin Oh (33) was invited by Jaehyun Park (38), an older friend from a close neighborhood social group, to join a coin funding deal. The group had existed for five years, and Jaehyun was known there as someone working at an IT company. Jaehyun said a contact had secured a token pre-round slot and that close friends could enter together. The structure was that Jaehyun had secured a KRW 150 million slot in a 100-person pool, would put in KRW 100 million himself, and would split the remaining KRW 50 million between two younger friends. Jungmin's share was KRW 25 million, and Jaehyun would receive the tokens under his own name and later remit each person's share. He said separate KYC for each person would take too long. Jaehyun added that someone at his company had worked with the issuing team, that the line was good, the pre-round price was about 60% of normal, the lockup was only 30 days, and friends had made 1.5 to 2 times returns in similar lines last year. The group chat had previously shown two screenshots where Jaehyun proved profits from other lines. Jungmin felt pressured by Jaehyun saying he was taking special care of him and by loyalty to an older group friend. Jaehyun said the decision had to be made within the week because slots were leaving the pool. The payment destination was Jaehyun's own account, explained as a batch transfer to the token team. As lunch hour was ending, Jungmin remembered another group member briefly saying, 'Jaehyun's line is really good.'
core.question: Should Jungmin Oh transfer KRW 25 million to Jaehyun Park's personal account to join this coin pre-round group purchase?
core.surface_answer: Because five years of social trust, Jaehyun's IT-company background, last year's profit screenshots, and another member's support combine with market terms such as pre-round price and 30-day lockup, he transfers the money to Jaehyun's account within the week.
core.hidden_answer: He should immediately withhold payment and verify the token project, issuer, exchange listing schedule, and official channels; the formal pre-round agreement and whether his own KYC is possible; whether money sent to Jaehyun's personal account can be traced to the issuing team; whether receiving tokens under Jaehyun's name and redistributing shares is legal; and whether friendship and old profit screenshots are biased social proof.
hidden_reasoning: A personal-account payment followed by Jaehyun holding the token pool and remitting shares makes the entire recovery path depend on one person; see t-01.
Receiving tokens under someone else's name without personal KYC is far from normal pre-round procedure; see t-02.
Without external verification of the project, issuer, and listing schedule, the token itself may not be real; see t-03.
Friendship and profit screenshots are social proof but may omit loss cases; see t-04.

core.story: Kyung-hye Han (58) received a KakaoTalk message around 1 p.m. on a weekday. The sender profile showed the familiar name 'Jaeho,' her son's name, but the profile photo was the gray default image instead of his usual photo. The message said, 'Mom, it's me, Jaeho. My phone screen broke, so I'm messaging from a temporary phone. I unlocked KakaoTalk and am using it.' When she asked what happened, Jaeho replied that he urgently needed KRW 300,000 for a wedding cash gift that evening because a friend had not repaid him and his card was tied to the broken phone. He promised to send it back to her account tomorrow. Kyung-hye knew her son often forgot cards, so it sounded plausible. The account sent to her was 'Kookmin Bank 60X-xx-xx-XXX, account holder Jaeho Kim.' The name seemed subtly different from her son Jaeho Han, but the message flow felt natural. Another message arrived: 'Mom, I have to go to the wedding anyway and timing is bad. Please hurry. Reply on KakaoTalk if you can, but if not, just transfer it.' Kyung-hye normally spoke with her son every week and had spoken with him a few days earlier. She briefly considered calling his real number, but Jaeho preemptively wrote, 'I can't call now. It's a temporary phone, outgoing calls don't work. KakaoTalk only. Just KRW 300,000 quickly.' Lunch cleanup was finished, and the afternoon news began on the living-room TV.
core.question: Should Kyung-hye Han transfer KRW 300,000 to the account under the name 'Jaeho Kim'?
core.surface_answer: Because her son's name appears, the KakaoTalk exchange feels natural, and KRW 300,000 is not a large amount, she sends it and receives repayment tomorrow.
core.hidden_answer: She should immediately withhold payment and verify through a separate channel whether the sender is really her son, such as calling his real number or using family contacts; check whether the account holder Jaeho Kim matches her son's legal name and characters; and recognize that a temporary phone, inability to call, and KakaoTalk-only communication match common family-impersonation messenger phishing patterns warned about by Korean police and financial regulators.
hidden_reasoning: Default gray profile, temporary phone, inability to call, KakaoTalk-only contact, and urgent transfer form the standard family-impersonation messenger-phishing pattern; see t-01.
The surname mismatch between account holder Jaeho Kim and her son Jaeho Han is a clear authenticity signal; see t-02.
Calling her son's real number directly is the key verification step; see t-03.
The KRW 300,000 amount is a threshold designed to make users skip verification; see t-04.

core.story: Juhwan Lim (45) received a LinkedIn message from someone he did not know. The sender, David Coleman, introduced himself as 'International Trustee - Geneva Office' and wrote, 'I represent a private estate in dispute resolution stage. Your Korean residency profile matches the trustee's safe-keeping criteria for an interim period.' David said his client was a deceased American businessperson and that a junior inheritance dispute was in progress. During the dispute, USD 4.2 million had to be temporarily held under the name of an interim trustee by a trustworthy Korean resident for up to six months, with compensation of USD 110,000. The funds would be deposited into a Korean commercial-bank virtual account under the name 'Coleman Trustee Korea Liaison Office,' and Juhwan would become the named custodian. David sent an English Geneva Office letterhead Engagement Letter with logos resembling the UK Foreign Office and Swiss bar association. The only cost for the custodian was a Korean lawyer power-of-attorney registration fee of USD 2,800, paid upfront by the custodian and later settled from the compensation. The destination was a virtual account under the name of a Korean lawyer, and David requested a passport copy, resident registration card copy, account copy, and signature sample for identity verification. David wrote, 'Time-sensitive engagement. We've shortlisted 3 Korean residents and you are the preferred candidate. Decision required within 5 business days.' Juhwan rarely used LinkedIn and found it odd that his profile would be recommended as a trustworthy Korean resident, but the USD 110,000 compensation was very attractive.
core.question: Should Juhwan Lim pay the USD 2,800 power-of-attorney registration fee and accept the interim trustee custody request from Coleman Trustee Korea Liaison Office?
core.surface_answer: Because the English Geneva Office letterhead, foreign-ministry and bar-association logos, five-business-day deadline, and USD 110,000 compensation look attractive, and USD 2,800 is small compared with the fee, he pays the registration cost and accepts.
core.hidden_answer: He should immediately withhold payment and verify that David Coleman, Coleman Trustee Korea Liaison Office, and the named Korean lawyer are not confirmed in any bar association or international trust registry; that there is no mechanism where a LinkedIn profile randomly qualifies a Korean resident as a trustworthy custodian; that normal trust operations do not make the custodian pay upfront fees for later reimbursement; and that bulk collection of passport, ID, account, and signature samples matches identity-theft patterns. This is a variant of 419 advance-fee fraud.

An upfront fee paid by the custodian and later reimbursed is the core of 419 advance-fee fraud; see t-02.
Bulk requests for passport, resident ID, and signature samples create identity theft, account lending, and money-laundering intermediary risks; see t-03.
Geneva Office, foreign-ministry, and bar-association logos are surface authority signals and do not prove existence; see t-04.

core.story: Daeun Shim (33) received a KakaoTalk borrowing request from her high-school classmate Jiwoo Park (33). Jiwoo was a friend she saw once or twice a year at reunions, and they had no major conflicts after starting their careers. He wrote that he was sorry but suddenly needed a favor: because of a lump-sum hospital payment for his wife, could she lend him KRW 8 million just for this week? He promised to repay exactly on the 25th of next month, write a loan note, and pay 5% interest. Jiwoo had a stable job at a mid-sized company for seven years, had been married four years, and had bought an apartment on the outskirts of Seoul last year. He added that his account balance was temporarily short, but a company incentive would arrive within a month and he could repay enough. Daeun had about KRW 25 million available. KRW 8 million was not the majority of it, but it was not small. She had never seen fraud or money-dispute signals from Jiwoo, and he was trusted among classmates. At the next cafe table, another customer was entering household accounts on a laptop.
core.question: Should Daeun Shim accept Jiwoo Park's borrowing request and lend him KRW 8 million?
core.surface_answer: Because Jiwoo shows stability through job, marriage, and apartment ownership, and because he offers a loan note, 5% interest, and an exact repayment date, she accepts the request and transfers KRW 8 million.
core.hidden_answer: Before deciding, she should check how losing access to KRW 8 million would affect her own cash flow, how to secure legal enforceability through a standard loan note and possible notarization, how much relationship damage she can tolerate if a dispute occurs, and Jiwoo's repayment capacity, including job stability, assets, and existing debts.
hidden_reasoning: Loans to acquaintances can have low recovery rates even with a loan note and interest agreement, and relationship loss is added if a dispute occurs; see t-01.
Locking KRW 8 million out of KRW 25 million requires checking emergency funds and living-cost impact; see t-02.
Daeun has limited directly verifiable information about Jiwoo's repayment capacity; see t-03.

core.story: Jisoo Won (28) saw a post in an internet community she often visited. The author said they had rescued an animal and were temporarily fostering it but lacked money for medical costs. The post included both a Kakao payment link and a bank account number. It showed one animal photo and one receipt photo, and said, 'Any help is appreciated. Even KRW 10,000 or 20,000 per person is a big help.' Jisoo had occasionally donated KRW 10,000 to posts like this before, and the comments included two short replies saying 'deposit complete.' Some small text on the receipt photo was hard to read, and the author's nickname was one she had never seen in the community before.
core.question: Should Jisoo Won donate KRW 10,000 to the provided account?
core.surface_answer: Because KRW 10,000 is a small amount, there are deposit-complete comments, and donating is a good act, she sends the money.
core.hidden_answer: Before sending, she should check the author's community activity history, the authenticity of the receipt photo and the animal hospital, and whether the same photo or receipt has appeared in other communities through reverse image search. Even though KRW 10,000 is small, the same pattern run across many boards can become cumulative small-amount fraud.
hidden_reasoning: If the author is a new nickname and the receipt or photo lacks external verification, the post may be part of a donation scam using the same photos across multiple communities; see t-01.
KRW 10,000-level cumulative fraud is hard to detect and uses an amount small enough for victims to skip verification; see t-02.
